claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure.
The starting alloy contains a continuous brittle ordered phase.
The continuous brittle phase causes dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries.
Boundary-associated dislocation pile-ups produce local stress concentrations and premature microcracking.
Solutionizing, water quenching, and low-temperature annealing can invert a continuous ordered phase into discrete nanoscale ordered precipitates in a continuous disordered or weakly ordered matrix.
High-temperature solutionizing dissolves the continuous brittle phase.
Rapid quenching suppresses unwanted coarse segregation.
Annealing near 600 °C can precipitate fine, discrete ordered phases after solutionizing and quenching.
Room-temperature quasi-static mechanical testing is applicable to evaluating the proposed treatment.
The desired structural mediator is a discontinuous nanoscale population of ordered precipitates embedded in a continuous ductile matrix.
Breaking up the continuous brittle phase permits a more uniform distribution of deformation.
In the inverted microstructure, dislocations can traverse the ductile matrix instead of piling up at large internal boundaries.
Reduced dislocation pile-up lowers local stress concentrations and suppresses microcrack initiation.
Dispersed ordered precipitates provide precipitation hardening.
The treatment will produce a significant, potentially several-fold increase in room-temperature tensile failure strain.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The untreated alloy undergoes catastrophic tensile fracture because of dislocation pile-ups at continuous brittle-phase boundaries.
Treatment effectiveness depends on temperature, duration, composition, and successful inversion of phase topology.
Performance under non-quasi-static loading has not been established.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant ductility improvement without strength loss, or failure to invert the phase topology, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is called a single-step heat treatment, but it explicitly comprises three sequential processing operations: solutionizing, quenching, and annealing/tempering.
